newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican separatists mount 61-bomb show of force.
newsitem.headline: Corsican separatists mount 61-bomb show of force.

text.p: Corsican separatist guerrillas exploded 61 bombs on the Mediterranean island on Sunday in a show of strength defying a French government crackdown.

No one was injured in the coordinated pre-dawn blitz and damage was mostly limited to smashed windows or damaged doorways at post offices, tax offices and other symbols of French state authority in towns and villages.

The outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) Historic Wing, seeking to prove it had not been crushed by the detention of three political leaders, said it planted the 61 bombs and six others that failed to explode.

"The future lies in struggle," it said in a statement, accusing the centre-right French government of betrayal by switching to repression from talks. "We will have multiple struggles, both in Corsica and in Europe."

It was the most violent night on the tourist island of 250,000 people since the Resistenza separatist group staged 50 blasts and attempted bombings on February 9 last year. More than 100 bombs exploded on one night in August 1982.

Police in the northern town of Ghisonaccia detained three suspected separatists for questioning about Sunday's blasts, which defied heavy police reinforcements and government pledges to end 20 years of violence on Corsica.

Most bombs went off in remote rural areas where gendarmes mount only sporadic patrols. Investigators estimated that 120 to 150 people were involved in the attacks, planting sticks of dynamite with slow-burning fuses.

Corsican guerrillas have never been taken as seriously as Irish Republican Army guerrillas in Northern Ireland or ETA Basque separatists in Spain, partly because they seek to avoid casualties and are deeply divided over tactics and goals.
Opinion polls show most people on Corsica, the birthplace of Napoleon, do not want full independence but many favour the separatist goals of a greater role for the Corsican language and culture.
The FLNC Historic Wing's statement denounced the rival FLNC "Normal Wing" for announcing last week that was renouncing violence and would rely on political campaigns to press its claims for autonomy.

The FLNC Historic Wing is also active in mainland France. Its statement said it planted a bomb at a post office in the Riviera capital of Nice on Thursday and it had previously claimed a bomb at an Air France office in the town on Tuesday.

Most of Sunday's bombs exploded in northern Corsica between 4.30 a.m. and 5.30 a.m. (0330 and 0430 GMT), targeting 13 post offices, half a dozen tax offices, state-run banks, chambers of commerce, two Air France offices and other state-run buildings.
Three unoccupied private villas were also damaged. The northern town of Bastia was hardest hit with 15 blasts while one bomb went off in Ajaccio, Corsica's main town.

Francois Santoni, the head of the FLNC's political wing A Cuncolta, gave himself up in December and is in police detention on suspicion of involvement in extortion and bomb attacks. Two other Cuncolta leaders are also in detention.
